Quick Read

Ken Griffin declared an AI bubble, yet NVDA fell just 0.29% and QQQ slid 0.10%, with NVDA rebounding 2% in after-hours trading.

Griffin warned corporate America has struggled to extract value from AI, a spending slowdown that threatens Nvidia's $279 billion in supply commitments.

Agentic AI tools cut Citadel research from 6 weeks to 2 hours, shifting Griffin from dismissive in January to unsettled by May 2026.

Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor)

Ken Griffin changed his mind about artificial intelligence more than once in 2026. On October 20, 2026, at Citadel's annual Future of Global Markets Conference in New York, the Citadel founder and CEO said investors are "almost certainly" in an AI bubble.

Larry Busacca / Getty Images

The market barely responded. After the close, NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) ended at $216.47, off 0.29%, before climbing 2.12% to $221.06 by 7:59 p.m. ET in after-hours trading. The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) slid 0.10% to $717.63. That calm looks reasonable once you read past the word bubble.

NVDA Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.
Griffin Ties Bubbles to Lasting Economic Change

Griffin tied bubbles to real economic change: "Any radical transformation of our economy is generally intertwined with a bubble."

He said the companies that make it through "are the market leaders for decades to come." Remembering the dot-com era, he added, "I just wish I'd kept my Amazon stock in that moment."

Money tends to arrive before the profits do, and while most new entrants fail, a few survivors keep growing for a generation.

Mixed AI Payoffs Would Reach Chipmakers First

His more pointed warning was about returns. "Corporate America has been very uneven in its ability to extract value from its AI models," he said. He described finance teams reviewing bills from Anthropic and OpenAI and concluding, "Okay, we need to think about how to make sure we're getting productivity out of this."

Image by Rob Hayek via 24/7 Wall Street

A surge this large from a mature consumer staple puts shareholders in a tough spot. The hold case rests on Coca-Cola's defensive appeal, but a gain this large leaves less room for disappointment, the heart of the profit-taking argument.

Coca-Cola Outruns Its Beverage Rivals

Coca-Cola stock has pulled well ahead of its two closest beverage peers. Notably, PepsiCo (NASDAQ:PEP) stock is down 3% to $134.46 YTD. Monster Beverage (NASDAQ:MNST) stock is up 23% to $46.98 YTD, still behind Coca-Cola.

Each company runs a distinct business model. For its part, Coca-Cola sells concentrate and syrups to bottlers and owns brands including Sprite, Fanta, Powerade and BODYARMOR, while PepsiCo pairs beverages with a large snack business. Energy drinks are the focus at Monster.

Defensive Demand Explains Only Part of the Rally

A search for steadier names has supported consumer staples this year. The Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSEARCA:XLP) is up 15% to $87.59 YTD, short of the gain in Coca-Cola stock. Coca-Cola shares made up 6.8% of the fund's net assets as of June 30, one of its largest positions.
